from.place: Proof paragraph 2, the three displayed derived Hom objects: generic dg-quotient infrastructure through the recorded ancestry, specifically the finite-cone argument in the final step of lem-coef-dg-quotient-hom-cone. The triangulated structure is obtained from a general cone-closed module-category criterion, before proving invariance of the finite hull. Abstract dg-category axioms (A), (B), (C) supply the generic triangulation theorem used after the module and sign checks. Technical input: Admissible quotients of a three-object dg flag.

title: Admissible quotients of a three-object dg flag
statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be a small cochain dg category over $\mathbf Z$ (a set of objects, cochain complexes of abelian groups $\mathcal A(x,y)$ as morphism objects, and associative unital compositions $\mathcal A(y,z)\otimes\mathcal A(x,y)\to\mathcal A(x,z)$ which are chain maps, so that $\partial(gh)=(\partial g)h+(-1)^{|g|}g\partial h$ for homogeneous $g,h$), with Hom differential $\partial$. Write $Z^0\mathcal A$ for closed degree-zero maps and $H^0\mathcal A$ for their classes modulo degree-minus-one boundaries. Assume (A) a zero object and dg binary sums, whose inclusions and projections are closed degree-zero maps satisfying the biproduct identities. Assume (B) dg functors $[n]$, $n\in\mathbf Z$, with $[0]=1$, $[n+m]=[n][m]$, and composition-compatible cochain isomorphisms $\mathcal A(x,y[n])\cong\mathcal A(x,y)[n]$, where $V[n]^j=V^{j+n}$ and $d_{V[n]}=(-1)^nd_V$. A sequence $u\xrightarrow{a}v\xrightarrow{b}w$ in $Z^0\mathcal A$ is called admissible when there are graded degree-zero maps $\pi:v\to u$ and $s:w\to v$ such that $\pi a=1$, $bs=1$, $a\pi+sb=1$, $ba=0$, and $\pi s=0$; its boundary is the closed map $\delta=\pi\partial s:w\to u[1]$ under (B). A map is an admissible monomorphism if it is the first arrow of such a sequence. Assume (C) that each closed degree-zero $f:x\to y$ has an admissible sequence $y\xrightarrow{i_f}c(f)\xrightarrow{p_f}x[1]$ with boundary $f[1]$. A homotopy equivalence is a closed degree-zero map with a closed degree-zero inverse modulo boundaries. Let $x\xrightarrow{\alpha}y\xrightarrow{\beta}z$ be admissible monomorphisms. Choose admissible sequences $x\xrightarrow{\alpha}y\xrightarrow{p_1}q_1$ and $y\xrightarrow{\beta}z\xrightarrow{p_3}q_3$, with graded splittings $(\pi_1,s_1)$ and $(\pi_3,s_3)$ and boundaries $\delta_1:q_1\to x[1]$, $\delta_3:q_3\to y[1]$. There is an admissible sequence $x\xrightarrow{\beta\alpha}z\xrightarrow{p_2}q_2$ with graded splitting $(\pi_2,s_2)$ for which $\pi_2=\pi_1\pi_3$. Write $\delta_2:q_2\to x[1]$ for its boundary. The maps $u=p_2\beta s_1:q_1\to q_2$ and $v=p_3s_2:q_2\to q_3$ are closed degree-zero maps, and $q_1\xrightarrow{u}q_2\xrightarrow{v}q_3$ is admissible with graded splitting $r=p_1\pi_3s_2$, $t=p_2s_3$. Its boundary $r\partial t$ is $p_1[1]\delta_3:q_3\to q_1[1]$. In $H^0\mathcal A$ the four identities $up_1=p_2\beta$, $\delta_2u=\delta_1$, $vp_2=p_3$, and $\delta_3v=\alpha[1]\delta_2$ hold. No triangulated-category axiom is assumed.

source.place: Tag 09QX, lemma-dgc-analogue-tr4 and its displayed quotient construction; correct the typos s_2 p_2=0 and pi_3 beta=0 in the proof to s_2 p_2=1-beta alpha pi_1 pi_3 and pi_3 beta=1.

proof.text: Use right-to-left composition and work first with homogeneous maps in the unshifted Hom complexes. Chain-map composition, as recalled in the statement, means $\partial(gh)=(\partial g)h+(-1)^{|g|}g\partial h$. For any admissible splitting $(a,b,\pi,s)$ put $D=\pi\partial s$, of degree $1$. Differentiating $bs=1$ and using $1=a\pi+sb$ gives $\partial s=aD$. Differentiating $1=a\pi+sb$ and multiplying on the left by $\pi$ gives $\partial\pi=-Db$. Consequently $\partial D=(\partial\pi)\partial s=-DbaD=0$. Under (B), $D$ represents the closed degree-zero boundary. Apply this calculation to the two given sequences to obtain $D_1=\pi_1\partial s_1$, $D_3=\pi_3\partial s_3$, $\partial s_1=\alpha D_1$, $\partial\pi_1=-D_1p_1$, $\partial s_3=\beta D_3$, and $\partial\pi_3=-D_3p_3$.

source.place: Tag 09P6, lemma-get-triangle, identities (1)-(8), expanded directly from the dg composition and splitting definitions.

proof.text: The degree-one map $E=p_1D_3:q_3\to q_1$ is closed since $p_1$ and $D_3$ are closed. Let $\varepsilon:q_3\to q_1[1]$ be its degree-zero version under (B), so $\varepsilon=p_1[1]\delta_3$. Set $f=\varepsilon[-1]:q_3[-1]\to q_1$. It is closed because $[-1]$ is a dg functor; the strict shift identities give $f[1]=\varepsilon$. Apply the ASSUMED axiom (C) to $f$ to choose $q_2=c(f)$ and an admissible sequence $q_1\xrightarrow{j}q_2\xrightarrow{k}q_3$, with graded splitting $(R,T)$, whose boundary is exactly $\varepsilon$. No existence of a graded kernel or additional quotient object is being assumed.

source.place: Tag 09QJ, situation-ABC, axiom (C); construction filling the omitted existence argument at the start of Tag 09QX, lemma-dgc-analogue-tr4.

proof.text:
The chosen sequence has $Rj=1$, $kT=1$, $jR+Tk=1$, $kj=0$, and $RT=0$. The calculation of step 1, with its prescribed boundary $E$, gives $\partial T=jE$ and $\partial R=-Ek$. Define graded degree-zero maps
$$P=jp_1\pi_3+Tp_3:z\to q_2,\qquad S=\beta s_1R+s_3k:q_2\to z,\qquad \Pi=\pi_1\pi_3:z\to x.$$
The identities $\pi_3\beta=1$, $\pi_3s_3=0$, $p_3\beta=0$, $p_3s_3=1$, $p_1\alpha=0$, and $\pi_1s_1=0$ give $\Pi\beta\alpha=1$, $P\beta\alpha=0$, and $\Pi S=0$ by direct substitution.

source.place: Tag 09QX, lemma-dgc-analogue-tr4, quotient diagrams; explicit cone-based formulas for the middle quotient.

proof.text:
Expand the other two graded splitting equations:
$$PS=jp_1s_1R+Tp_3s_3k=jR+Tk=1,$$
with the two cross terms zero by $\pi_3s_3=0$ and $p_3\beta=0$. In the other order the two cross terms vanish by $RT=0$ and $kj=0$, and
$$SP=\beta s_1p_1\pi_3+s_3p_3=\beta(1-\alpha\pi_1)\pi_3+s_3p_3=1-\beta\alpha\Pi.$$
Thus the underlying graded sequence $x\xrightarrow{\beta\alpha}z\xrightarrow{P}q_2$ has precisely the required splitting $(\Pi,S)$.

source.place: Tag 09QX, lemma-dgc-analogue-tr4, graded direct-sum argument, here replaced by its explicit inverse-map equations.

proof.text:
The quotient map $P$ is closed:
$$\partial P=jp_1\partial\pi_3+(\partial T)p_3=-jp_1D_3p_3+jEp_3=0.$$
Also $\beta\alpha$ is closed as the composite of closed maps. Therefore the graded splitting of step 4 is an admissible sequence in $Z^0\mathcal A$. Take $p_2=P$, $s_2=S$, and $\pi_2=\Pi=\pi_1\pi_3$. Its boundary is closed by step 1. This establishes the existence of the composite quotient with the specified retraction, from the cone axiom alone.

source.place: Tag 09QX, lemma-dgc-analogue-tr4, existence of the second quotient; closedness verified using Tag 09P6 identities.

proof.text:
Compute its boundary explicitly. The Leibniz rule and step 3 give
$$\partial S=\beta\alpha D_1R-\beta s_1Ek+\beta D_3k.$$
Because $E=p_1D_3$ and $1-s_1p_1=\alpha\pi_1$, this becomes
$$\partial S=\beta\alpha(D_1R+\pi_1D_3k).$$
Multiplying by $\Pi$, for which $\Pi\beta\alpha=1$, shows that the degree-one version of $\delta_2$ is
$$D_2=\Pi\partial S=D_1R+\pi_1D_3k.$$
This is an equality of homogeneous maps, before passing to $H^0$.

source.place: Tag 09QX, lemma-dgc-analogue-tr4, boundary of the composite quotient, expanded via Tag 09P6.

proof.text:
The four maps in the statement are the original cone splitting maps. Indeed
$$u=P\beta s_1=jp_1s_1=j,\qquad v=p_3S=p_3s_3k=k,$$
$$r=p_1\pi_3S=p_1s_1R=R,\qquad t=Ps_3=Tp_3s_3=T.$$
Every omitted summand is zero by $p_3\beta=0$ or $\pi_3s_3=0$. Thus $u,v$ are closed, and all five admissibility equations for $(u,v,r,t)$ are the five equations listed in step 3. In particular $vu=kj=0$.

source.place: Tag 09QX, lemma-dgc-analogue-tr4, dashed arrows and their graded splitting; corrected calculation of their zero composite.

proof.text:
The boundary of $q_1\xrightarrow{u}q_2\xrightarrow{v}q_3$ is
$$r\partial t=R\partial T=RjE=E=p_1D_3,$$
which corresponds under (B) to $p_1[1]\delta_3$, as claimed. Equivalently, the source's final calculation is $p_1\pi_3(1-\beta\alpha\pi_1\pi_3)\partial s_3=p_1\pi_3\partial s_3$, because $p_1\pi_3\beta\alpha=p_1\alpha=0$, using $\pi_3\beta=1$. This calculation uses $s_2p_2=1-\beta\alpha\pi_1\pi_3$, not the erroneous zero identity printed earlier in the source.

source.place: Tag 09QX, lemma-dgc-analogue-tr4, final displayed calculation, with its two printed typos corrected.

proof.text:
Two of the four required squares commute strictly:
$$up_1=jp_1=P\beta,\qquad vp_2=kP=p_3,$$
by the formulas for $P$ and $kT=1$, $kj=0$, $\pi_3\beta=1$, $p_3\beta=0$. A third commutes strictly after the shift identification: step 6 gives
$$D_2u=(D_1R+\pi_1D_3k)j=D_1,$$
since $Rj=1$ and $kj=0$. Hence $\delta_2u=\delta_1$ already among closed maps, and all three identities hold in $H^0\mathcal A$.

source.place: Tag 09QX, lemma-dgc-analogue-tr4, the three octahedral squares computed from the displayed quotient maps.

proof.text:
For the last square the necessary homotopy is explicit. Set $h=s_1R:q_2\to y$, a graded degree-zero map. Then
$$\partial h=\alpha D_1R-s_1Ek,$$
whereas $1-\alpha\pi_1=s_1p_1$ and step 6 give
$$D_3v-\alpha D_2=s_1p_1D_3k-\alpha D_1R=-\partial h.$$
The cochain isomorphism $\mathcal A(q_2,y[1])\cong\mathcal A(q_2,y)[1]$ sends $h$ to degree $-1$ and has differential $-\partial$. Thus if $H$ is the corresponding degree-minus-one map into $y[1]$, the last displayed identity is exactly $\delta_3v-\alpha[1]\delta_2=\partial H$. It follows that $[\delta_3v]=[\alpha[1]\delta_2]$. This proves the fourth identity without assuming any triangulated-category axiom.

source.place: Tag 09QX, lemma-dgc-analogue-tr4, last octahedral square; explicit homotopy with the shift sign from axiom (B).
